recentItems.title: He held a knife to his abuser's throat. Then he took him to court. | Part 1 of 2
recentItems.description:
Willie Blackwater is just 13 when he holds a knife to his rapist's throat, demanding an end to his recurring abuse.  It’s the first time Willie stands up to his residential school supervisor, but it’s far from the last. Years later, after a fateful encounter with a cop, Willie decides to break his silence — joining a group of survivors that help convict Arthur Henry Plint of 18 counts of sexual assault.  

But for Willie and his friends, it’s not enough. And a risky idea starts to form.  Can they take on the architects of the residential school system?  


Host Falen Johnson and journalist Jackie McKay meet the man behind Blackwater vs. Plint, one of the first court cases where residential school survivors took their abuser to court, eventually paving a legal path for thousands of other Indigenous children forced to attend these schools. 

This episode is part one of two.

recentItems.title: He held a knife to his abuser's throat. Then he took him to court. | Part 2 of 2
recentItems.description:
Willie Blackwater’s abuser is in jail, but for him, justice hasn’t been served.  Twenty-eight of Arthur Henry Plint’s victims — including Willie — launch a civil suit to seek damages from the federal government and the United Church of Canada.  The trial to hold these authorities vicariously liable for the horrors of residential schools is brutal and explosive, and not everyone makes it out alive.  

Host Falen Johnson and journalist Jackie McKay trace Willie’s quest for justice as  Blackwater vs. Plint heads to the B.C. Supreme Court — a trial that exposes the widespread damage done by residential schools, and sets in motion the creation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

This episode is part two of two.

recentItems.title: Can Canada turn its airports into money-making machines? | About That
recentItems.description:

Andrew Chang breaks down how the country's airports rely so heavily on passengers to fund operations and explains the potential risks and benefits of Carney's proposal.
